page: Amazon Web Services i3en.xlarge is a storage-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. The platform features 4 vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores on an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor operating at a base clock speed of 3.1 GHz. The CPU architecture supports advanced instruction sets including AVX-512 and AES. Memory capacity is configured at 32 GB of DDR4 operating at 3 GHz, providing an 8 GB allocation per physical core. A defining feature of this instance is the bundled local storage, consisting of a 2,500 GB NVMe SSD. It provides a baseline network throughput of 4 Gbps and does not include GPU acceleration.

Benchmark results highlight an operational profile heavily weighted toward storage capacity and memory capacity rather than raw compute speed. In compute evaluations, the Intel Xeon 8259CL scored 3960.05 in PassMark CPU tests and 2250.0 in Geekbench multi-core, reflecting lower-quartile performance compared to compute-focused alternatives. Compression and decompression tests similarly show lower throughput, such as multi-threaded bzip3 decompression achieving 15.64 GB/sec. However, memory subsystems demonstrate stable execution, with PassMark memory scoring in the mid-range at 2086.11 and Redis SET operations achieving 3.28 million operations per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the hardware configuration optimizes resource density by pairing a large local NVMe volume with a moderate compute footprint. Deployments that require massive local disk space and standard memory allocation without high core counts achieve favorable cost-per-gigabyte characteristics. The primary tradeoff is the constrained processor performance, making it inefficient for CPU-heavy tasks such as compilation, physics calculations, or high-throughput machine learning inference. Amazon Web Services i3en.xlarge is best suited for I/O-heavy workloads, including distributed NoSQL databases, search indices, log analytics, and data warehousing nodes.

The instance integrates a large 2,500 GB local NVMe SSD, delivering high-capacity, low-latency storage directly attached to the host, while offering a baseline network speed of 4 Gbps without discrete GPU hardware. Benchmark results indicate modest computational throughput, with PassMark CPU scores and multi-threaded decompression falling into the lower quartile, balanced by average PassMark memory scores and Redis throughput of 3.28 million operations per second. This hardware balance positions the instance as a cost-efficient platform for local NVMe storage density rather than raw compute speed. It is best suited for storage-bound workloads, such as distributed databases, log aggregation, and data warehousing.
